title: Best Affirmation Apps for Fear of Failure and Self-Doubt in 2026
description: The best affirmation apps for fear of failure and self-doubt in 2026, compared by whether their sentences separate the attempt from the verdict, whether you can write one at a believable size in a kind voice, whether they reach you before the avoidance decision, and what they cost over a year — with the fear-of-failure appraisal, achievement-goal, self-compassion and positive-self-statement research, and Anicca, at 5.0 stars from 1 US rating, ranked sixth, not first.
markdown:
By Anicca · November 2026

"Best affirmation app" is the wrong question when what you actually have is not a shortage of talent but a draft you will not send. The application is finished, or finished enough. The portfolio exists. The message is written and sits unsent, and the reason is not laziness and it is not standards, exactly. It is a forecast. Before anything has happened, the mind has already run the failure and itemised its price: the embarrassment of being seen trying and falling short, the revision it would force in what you believe about yourself, the future it might close off, the interest other people might withdraw, the disappointment in a specific person's voice. So the safest available move presents itself as no move at all — or as its two disguises, choosing something so small it cannot count as a failure, or something so impossible that failing at it proves nothing. Then the second act arrives: the relief of not having risked it curdles, by evening, into evidence. *See. You did not even try.* The apps below are therefore not ranked by who promises you confidence, fearlessness or success. A sentence like "I am fearless, I always succeed" is, for this reader, the least believable sentence in the world, and unbelieved sentences do not sit quietly — they summon their counter-evidence. They are ranked by a narrower test: whether an app can put a sentence in front of you that separates the attempt from the verdict — a sentence about the next try, at a size you can believe, that does not make your worth, your future or other people's regard the stake of one ordinary Tuesday attempt. What follows is a comparison of self-help tools for the fear of failure, written for people who are not afraid of work, but of what a visible failure would mean.

This comparison follows the same form as our roundups of the best affirmation apps for anxiety, for sleep and racing thoughts at night, for self-esteem and low self-worth, for stress and overwhelm, for overthinking and rumination, for imposter syndrome and the fraud feeling at work, for perfectionism and the flawless-or-failure loop, for social anxiety and the replay after conversations, for burnout and exhaustion that rest does not fix, for a breakup and the urge to check their profile, for grief after the death of someone you love, for depression and persistently low mood, for people-pleasing and the fear of disapproval, for health anxiety and the search-check-reassure loop, for loneliness and the quiet room at night, for OCD and intrusive thoughts, for shame and guilt and the replay that turns an act into a verdict, for anger and irritability and the sixty seconds in which a feeling becomes a sentence someone else has to live with, and for procrastination and low motivation and the eleven-times-opened file, re-aimed at the fear of failure and the unsent draft. It is a different cut from two neighbours on that list, and the difference matters. Perfectionism is about the standard — nothing counts unless it is flawless. The imposter feeling is about the past — success has already happened and is being explained away. Fear of failure is about the future — a failure that has not happened is being priced in advance, in five specific currencies the research below names, and the price is being paid now, in attempts never made.

*Disclosure: Anicca, the app listed sixth here, is made by the team behind this site. It is not ranked first. No app paid to be here. Prices and ratings are from the US App Store listings when we last checked them on November 21, 2026; check the store page for your country. Two boundaries before the list itself. First: fear of failure is a pattern of appraisal, not a diagnosis, and self-doubt is a feeling, not a measurement — the research below finds that the fear tracks the consequences a person expects failure to carry, not their actual competence; in the founding measurement study it was unrelated to perceived competence. Second: no app on this page is a treatment for anything, including our own app. A fear of being judged that is narrowing your work, your studies or your life can sit inside larger things — social anxiety, depression, perfectionism with real clinical weight — and where avoidance is costing you a career, an education, health or relationships, or arrives with persistent low mood or thoughts of harming yourself, that is a reason to talk to a clinician, or, in a crisis, your local emergency number now — in the US, call or text 988, or 911 in an emergency; in Japan, call 110 or 119 in an emergency. And the boundary runs in the other direction too: sometimes the forecast is information. Some rooms really do punish a visible failure unfairly, some stakes really are high, and the honest sentence is not always "try anyway" — sometimes it is "this attempt, in this place, at this price, is not mine to make," said once, deliberately, rather than by default every day.*

## How we judged these, for fear of failure specifically

1. **Does the sentence separate the attempt from the verdict?** This is the first filter, and most affirmation content fails it. When researchers built the standard measure of fear of failure, it did not resolve into one fear but five appraisals of what failure would mean: experiencing shame and embarrassment, devaluing your own estimate of yourself, having an uncertain future, important others losing interest, and upsetting important others (Conroy, Willow & Metzler, 2002). Read against that finding, the test for an app is whether its sentences can address the attempt without raising the stakes of those five — not "I am a winner and everyone will see it," which welds the try to the verdict and to the audience, but "this draft goes out at ten; what it proves is that it went out." Apps whose words can be built at the size of an attempt rank above libraries of triumph.

2. **Can you write it yourself, at a believable size, in a kind voice?** Two findings meet here. Wood, Perunovic and Lee (2009) found that people with low self-esteem who repeated a large positive self-statement felt worse, because the gap summoned the counter-evidence — and on the morning of the unsent application, "I am fearless and unstoppable" is that sentence. And Neff, Hsieh and Dejitterat (2005) found that self-compassion was associated with less fear of failure and greater perceived competence, and through those, with goals aimed at learning rather than at defending self-worth. The grammar that survives a fearful morning is therefore small, specific and unpunishing: it names the attempt, it allows the attempt to go badly without a verdict, and it speaks to you the way you would speak to someone whose trying you actually wanted to protect. Apps that let you write, record and shrink a sentence rank above fixed libraries of large ones.

3. **Does it reach you before the avoidance decision, not after it?** Fear of failure does its work at a specific moment: the minute before the attempt, when the goal quietly converts from approaching something to avoiding a verdict. In a classroom study, performance-avoidance goals — trying not to look incompetent — were grounded in fear of failure and low expectations of competence, and they undermined both intrinsic motivation and actual graded performance (Elliot & Church, 1997). A later study following students over three weeks found fear of failure predicted change toward avoidance goals, not the reverse (Conroy & Elliot, 2004). The practical test is therefore placement and timing: a sentence already on your lock screen on the morning of the attempt, a reminder set for the hour of the interview rather than for a motivational morning in the abstract, a playlist that starts with one press when pressing send feels impossible. An app that helps only in a calm evening review is treating the hour when you least need it.

4. **What does it cost, and what does it cost you to come back after a failure?** Learning to attempt things under this fear is measured in months, not in a trial week, and a habit study at University College London found a new behaviour took a median of 66 days to feel automatic, with a range of 18 to 254 days (Lally et al., 2010). Judge every app on the long window: what it costs over a year, and whether returning after an actual failure — a rejection, a bad result, the thing itself, not a hypothetical — feels like resuming or like reporting to a second judge. An app that greets the week after a real failure with a broken streak and a lost medal has, for this reader, simply added a sixth appraisal to the original five.

## The six at a glance

| App | Best for | Standout | Get it |

## 1. Believe: Best for writing the attempt-sized sentence yourself, in your own voice

Believe takes first place here because question 1 is the whole game on this page, and Believe is the only app on this list built around letting you set the content of the claim yourself. You can **write your own affirmations**, **record them in your own voice**, and say them to your own face in the **Soul mirror**. That is how a sentence stops being a prophecy and becomes an instruction. Not "I am fearless, I succeed at everything I attempt," which the morning of the attempt will dismantle in seconds and bill you for the dismantling. Instead, the line written in the grammar the fear-of-failure research supports: one attempt, one hour, no verdict attached — "at ten I send the draft as it is; a refusal answers the draft, not my worth; the next attempt is Thursday's, whatever this one returns." Its listing organises words by the moment you are in, and the named categories include **work** and **study**, alongside self-love, relationships, confidence before a hard day, calm before sleep, gratitude, mornings, health, money, mindfulness and personal growth, and its current listing adds a free "Mental Health" category. **Timed sessions** with music and calming sounds give one line room to land, and widgets and scheduled reminders cover the timing of question 3 — a reminder set for the hour of the attempt, not for a generic morning, is a sentence you arranged before the forecast started pricing the day. Write the lines on a steadier day, write them about attempts rather than outcomes, and let each one end in a verb you control: send, submit, ask, show, try. You do not control accept, approve, admire — and a sentence that promises you the verbs you do not control is a sentence the fear can always collect on.

Believe launched in June 2021 and showed **4.9 stars from 379 US ratings** when we checked on November 21, 2026. Its US listing shows Believe Premium+ at **$3.99 a month** and a **lifetime option at $69.99** among its in-app purchases.

### Where it falls short

The crowd is elsewhere — 379 ratings against I am's hundreds of thousands. If social proof is your evidence, the evidence is not here. Believe also tracks consistency with practice medals, which cuts directly against question 4: for most people medals are decoration, but if a lost medal in the week after a real rejection would become one more verdict in a week already full of them, use the sessions and ignore the medals entirely. And the writing, the recording and the mirror all ask something of you up front, on a steadier day — including the hardest editorial decision on this page: the sentences have to be attempts, not prophecies and not threats. A line that rehearses the five appraisals ("if this fails, everyone will see I am not good enough") is the fear itself, recorded in your own voice. That is why Innertune, which asks for one press, is second on this page.

## 2. Innertune: Best for one press when composing anything is one risk too many

Innertune is the app for the morning when question 1 cannot even be attempted because the forecast is already loud and opening a blank editor feels like a second exposure. Its core practice requires, at the moment of use, exactly one press. Its listing opens with "Stop the negative thought spiral", builds **a personalised playlist for your exact situation** from **77,000 affirmations across 550+ playlists**, and is built to run while you sleep, work or relax. Unusually on this list, its listing names this page's problem in its own words: it says it is designed to help with anxiety and racing thoughts, sleep, **self-doubt and confidence**, and breaking negative thought patterns. For fear of failure, that passivity has one specific, honest use: it can lower the temperature in the hour before the attempt without asking you to author anything, perform anything or believe anything in particular first. You can also **record in your own voice** or choose from professional voices, and match the playlist with beats for focus, relaxation or sleep — which means the same tool that plays before the attempt can play, at a different setting, the evening after one goes badly, when the replay starts and the verdict is being drafted.

Innertune showed **4.8 stars from 12,177 US ratings** when we checked on November 21, 2026. Its US listing shows Innertune Premium at **$29.99 a year** and **$9.99 a month** among its in-app purchases.

### Where it falls short

A playlist is received, not written, and that is both its mercy and its ceiling. The sentences are sized by someone else, and some of them will be outcome sentences — success, achievement, winning — of exactly the kind question 2 warns about: heard on the wrong morning, at the wrong size, they can raise the stakes they were meant to lower. Skip without ceremony; a skipped track is not a failed practice. The personalisation also depends on the situation labels you choose, and there is no label that knows your five appraisals — which consequence *you* are pricing, shame or a person's disappointment or the uncertain future. Believe, where you write the sentence yourself, remains first for that reason. And a caution specific to this reader: listening can itself become the safe disguise, the preparation that never quite finishes. If the playlist ends and the draft is still unsent, the app has soothed the avoidance rather than interrupted it — set the attempt for the minute the playlist ends, while you are setting the playlist up.

## 3. I am: Best for a different sentence on the lock screen, at scale

I am is the scale answer, and for some readers scale is the point. It showed **4.8 stars from 739,855 US ratings** when we checked on November 21, 2026 — by far the largest body of evidence on this page that people keep an affirmation practice at all. Its model is placement: choose from a large library of daily intentions, put them on your **lock screen and widgets**, and set **reminders to be delivered throughout the day**, so a sentence arrives in the ordinary course of picking up your phone rather than inside a session you have to decide to begin. For fear of failure that placement matters in one specific way: the forecast does not only run before large, scheduled attempts. It runs in small moments all day — the email not opened, the hand not raised, the question not asked in the meeting. A sentence that is simply *there*, at phone-pickup, dozens of times a day, is aimed at that background pricing in a way a morning session is not. Its library is organised by the areas of life you want to work on, and the sheer size of the library means the reader who needs the attempt-sized sentence — about trying, learning, beginning — can usually find one nearer their size than the flagship claims about capability and dreams.

I am's US listing shows I am Premium at **$59.99 a year**, **$14.99 a month** and a **lifetime option at $89.99** among its in-app purchases, checked on November 21, 2026.

### Where it falls short

The library's centre of gravity is the large positive claim — capability, abundance, the amazing day — and Wood, Perunovic and Lee's finding is the standing warning for this page: for the reader whose self-estimate is currently low, the largest sentences are the ones most likely to summon the counter-argument, and the counter-argument, rehearsed daily, is practice too, in the wrong direction. The work with I am is therefore curation, done on a steadier day: favour the sentences about process and permission, mute the ones about outcomes and other people's admiration, and treat any sentence that makes you argue as data, not as resistance to push through. You also cannot write the attempt sentence in your own words and your own voice the way Believe and ThinkUp allow, which is why, on a page where the exact wording is the intervention, the largest library ranks third rather than first.

## 4. Gratitude: Best for a written record of attempts — including the ones that failed

Gratitude earns its place on this page for a tool that is not, strictly, an affirmation feature at all: the **private journal**. Fear of failure maintains itself partly through bookkeeping. The mind keeps a meticulous ledger of failures — dated, detailed, cross-referenced — and a vague, easily-lost sense of attempts. A journal with **prompts**, kept privately, reverses the bookkeeping: it is where the attempt gets recorded at its true size ("sent the application Tuesday; heard nothing; the nothing was about the application") before the verdict enlarges it. Gratitude pairs that journal with **hundreds of affirmations you can listen to or read**, the ability to **write your own affirmations and record your voice** to them, a **vision board**, and reminders with prompts to help build the journaling habit. Used for this page's purpose, the vision board needs one discipline: board the attempts, not only the outcomes. A board that holds only the accepted, the won and the arrived is a gallery of verdicts, and on the morning of a new attempt it prices the attempt against a wall of other people's finished stories. A board that also holds the tries — the submitted, the asked, the shown — is a record that trying is what this life actually consists of. The journal is also, after an actual failure, the one tool on this page designed for the evening itself: writing what happened, what it does and does not revise, and what the next attempt is, while the event is still a fact and before it hardens into an identity.

Gratitude showed **4.9 stars from 44,998 US ratings** when we checked on November 21, 2026. Its US listing shows an **annual pro plan at $29.99** and a **monthly pro plan at $4.99** among its in-app purchases.

### Where it falls short

Journaling is writing, and writing is itself an attempt that can be feared, graded and avoided — the blank entry can become one more unsent draft. The prompts help, and the honest instruction is the same as everywhere on this page: the entry is three lines, badly written, about facts. Gratitude also keeps a **journal streak**, which is question 4's hazard in its purest form: a streak broken in the week of a real failure teaches exactly the lesson this page exists to unteach, that a gap is a verdict. Ignore the streak; the record matters, the unbrokenness does not. And the affirmation side, while it allows your own words, is one feature among several in a broader self-care tool — if the single thing you need is the attempt sentence in your own voice on a loop before the moment, ThinkUp's narrower tool, next, is built more directly for it.

## 5. ThinkUp: Best for your own voice reading the attempt plan, on a loop, before the moment

ThinkUp is built around a single mechanism: **record affirmations in your own voice**, add music, and **play them in a loop** — its listing advises listening to the same set for at least 21 days, in sessions of at least five minutes, morning and before sleep. You **select from an expert-approved list or create your own**, build a programme around a goal, and set notifications to listen daily. Its named goal areas include motivation, self-esteem, a new career and achieving goals — the territories where fear of failure does most of its pricing. For this reader the mechanism has a specific virtue the libraries cannot match: the voice making the attempt-sized claim is yours, recorded on a steadier day, and it can be timed. Build the programme for the hour before — the commute before the interview, the morning of the submission, the walk before the presentation — and let the loop say the sentence you wrote when you could think clearly: what the attempt is, what it is not, what happens on Thursday regardless of what happens today. A free version lets you record up to three affirmations, which, honestly used, is enough for this page's entire method: one sentence for before the attempt, one for the minute after a setback, one for the evening replay.

ThinkUp showed **4.7 stars from 7,524 US ratings** when we checked on November 21, 2026. Its US listing prices Premium at **$7.99 a month**, **$39.99 a year** and **$99.99 for life**.

### Where it falls short

ThinkUp's framing leans toward manifestation and the large outcome — "manifest your dreams into reality" is its own language — and its expert lists include the triumph-sized sentences this page keeps warning about. The tool is excellent; the default content needs the same editorial discipline as everywhere else, and the recording session itself has to happen on a steadier day, because recording "I always succeed" in your own voice on a fearful morning is just the forecast with better production. The 21-day same-set instruction also deserves a caveat from this page's research: repetition is the mechanism, but a sentence that has started to summon arguments should be re-sized, not repeated harder. And its rating, 4.7 stars, is the lowest headline score among the six here — a small difference, but on a page committed to printing numbers as they are, it is printed.

## 6. Anicca: Best for one short card, no streak, nothing to fall behind on

Anicca is our app, it is listed sixth, and its numbers are printed at the same size as everyone else's: it showed **5.0 stars from 1 US rating** and **4.5 stars from 48 ratings in Japan** when we checked on November 21, 2026. One rating is not evidence of anything except newness, and this page does not pretend otherwise. What Anicca is, in its own store words, is an affirmation app **"made for anxious, overthinking minds"**: a **new affirmation on your Lock Screen every day**, **short cards you swipe through at your own pace**, favourites you can save, and gentle notifications — no programme to build, no library to curate, no session to complete, and no streak to break. For this page's reader, that smallness is the whole argument and also the whole limitation. The argument: on the morning of the attempt, Anicca asks nothing of you before it helps — no writing, no recording, no choosing — and the sentence is already where your eyes go when you pick up the phone to avoid the thing. A short line at a believable size, seen in passing, is sometimes the only size of help a fearful morning can accept without turning the help itself into another performance to fail at. After a failure, there is likewise nothing in Anicca to report to: no medal lost, no streak ended, no programme fallen behind on. You simply get tomorrow's card.

Anicca is free to download for iPhone. Its US listing shows **$14.99 a month** and **$59.99 a year** among its in-app purchases, checked on November 21, 2026.

### Where it falls short

Almost everything the top of this list can do, Anicca cannot. You cannot write the attempt sentence in your own words, record it in your own voice, build a playlist for the hour before, or keep a journal of attempts beside the words. Its library is small, its audience is small, its evidence base — one US rating — is the smallest on this page by an enormous distance, and it is iPhone only. If you need the sentence written for your specific attempt, Believe is the better tool and is ranked first for exactly that reason. Anicca's claim is narrower: for the reader whose fear attaches even to the tools — who has failed at meditation programmes, broken journal streaks and abandoned three affirmation apps by February — a single daily line with nothing to fall behind on may be the one form of the practice that survives contact with an actual failure. That is a real claim, and it is a small one, and both halves of that sentence are the review.

## Also worth knowing: Mantra

Mantra showed **4.8 stars from 34,496 US ratings** when we checked on November 21, 2026, with Premium at **$4.99 a month** and **$29.99 a year** in its US listing. It offers more than a thousand "I am" affirmations across 30+ categories, smart daytime and bedtime reminders, the ability to **add your own affirmations** and **record your voice and listen on repeat**, and guided sessions. It is a reasonable middle option — more personal than I am, less focused than Believe — and it is not in the six above for one reason specific to this page: its centre of gravity is the "I am" identity claim, and identity claims ("I am a winner", "I am unstoppable") are precisely the sentence-form that fear of failure prices highest and believes least. A reader who curates it toward process sentences will be well served; a reader who takes its defaults on a fearful morning may be handed the verdict grammar in a pleasant font.

## What the research actually says about fear of failure

The honest summary is that fear of failure is well measured, its mechanism is reasonably well understood, and no study anywhere in this section tested an affirmation app. What the research gives this page is not proof that any app works. It gives the shape of the problem, precisely enough to judge tools against — and it gives several warnings that the tools' own marketing will not give you.

**It is not one fear; it is five prices.** Conroy, Willow and Metzler (2002) built the Performance Failure Appraisal Inventory from interviews with performers and tested it in 544 college students. The 25-item measure resolved into five beliefs about what failing means: that it brings shame and embarrassment, that it requires you to lower your estimate of yourself, that it makes your future uncertain, that important others lose interest, and that important others are upset. Two details in that study deserve their prominence on this page. The first is that general fear of failure was *unrelated to perceived competence* — the fear is not a reading of ability, and more ability does not, by itself, retire it, which is why accomplished people sit unsent drafts too. The second is that the fear was associated with high worry and cognitive disruption: the forecast does not merely discourage, it occupies the mind that the attempt would need.

**The fear converts goals into avoidance, and avoidance performs worse.** Elliot and Church (1997), studying 178 undergraduates in a college classroom, tested a hierarchical model in which performance-avoidance goals — the goal of not looking incompetent — were grounded in fear of failure and low competence expectancies. Mastery goals, aimed at learning, supported intrinsic motivation; performance-avoidance goals undermined both intrinsic motivation and graded performance. The cruelty of the pattern is arithmetical: the strategy adopted to protect the result degrades the result, and then the degraded result is filed as evidence that the fear was accurate. Conroy and Elliot (2004) then followed 356 students across four occasions in three weeks and found the arrow points the way this page assumes: fear of failure predicted later change in mastery-avoidance and performance-avoidance goals, while goal scores did not reliably predict later change in the fear. The fear is upstream. Interventions — including sentences — belong upstream of the goal-setting, in the appraisal itself.

**Kindness is not the soft option; in the data it is the upstream one.** Neff, Hsieh and Dejitterat (2005) ran two studies of undergraduates — 222 in the first, and 110 in the second who perceived their recent midterm grade as a failure. Self-compassion was positively associated with mastery goals and negatively associated with performance goals, and the relationship was *mediated by lesser fear of failure* and greater perceived competence. Among the students who had just failed, self-compassion was also associated with emotion-focused coping and against avoidance-oriented coping. Read carefully, this is an associational finding, not a trial of an intervention — but it identifies the exact junction this page's second judging question is about. The sentence that treats a failure as an event in a shared human life, rather than as a verdict on a self, is associated with less of the fear itself, not merely with feeling nicer while afraid.

**Large positive sentences can backfire, measurably.** Wood, Perunovic and Lee (2009) showed that among people with low self-esteem, repeating a positive self-statement ("I'm a lovable person") or focusing only on how it was true left them feeling *worse* than controls, while people with high self-esteem benefited slightly. The authors' explanation — a statement outside a person's latitude of acceptance summons its own refutation — is the single most useful sentence-level finding for anyone choosing affirmations under self-doubt. It does not say affirmations are useless. It says size is a safety property: the sentence must be near enough to what you already half-believe that your mind does not immediately open the case against it. "I can send one imperfect draft" is inside most latitudes. "I am fearless" is inside very few.

**And time is the medium, whatever the tool.** Lally and colleagues (2010) tracked real habit formation and found a median of 66 days for a new behaviour to feel automatic, with a range of 18 to 254 days, and that missing an occasion did not doom the process. For this reader that last detail may be the most important number on the page: an actual failure — the rejection, the bad result — is, in habit terms, a missed occasion, not a reset. Any tool, sentence or system that treats it as a reset is contradicting the best time-course evidence we have.

None of this makes an app a treatment. Fear of failure that is costing you work, education, health or relationships — or that travels with persistent low mood, panic, or thoughts of harming yourself — deserves a clinician, and in a crisis your local emergency number: in the US, call or text 988, or 911 in an emergency; in Japan, call 110 or 119 in an emergency.

## How to choose, and a seven-day test that respects the evidence

Choose by the moment you are actually losing. If your unsent drafts die in the writing — if the forecast is loudest while you compose — choose **Believe**, and spend one steadier session writing three attempt sentences in your own voice. If composing anything is itself the exposure, choose **Innertune** and let one press carry the hour before, with the attempt scheduled for the minute the playlist ends. If the pricing runs all day in small moments, choose **I am** and curate it, on a calm day, toward process sentences. If your ledger is the problem — failures remembered in detail, attempts forgotten — choose **Gratitude** and keep the three-line record. If a specific recurring moment is the wall, choose **ThinkUp** and build the loop for the hour before it. If every system you have tried has itself become something to fail at, choose **Anicca** and take the one card a day, with nothing to fall behind on.

Then test any of them the same way, for seven days, at attempt size. Each morning, name one attempt — sendable, showable, askable — small enough that its failure would be an event, not a verdict. Put the app's sentence where it will be seen before the attempt, not after. Make the attempt before noon if you can; the forecast compounds with interest across a day. Each evening, record three facts only: the attempt, what actually happened, and what it actually revised — which is usually, in the research's terms, far less than the five prices quoted in advance. On the day an attempt genuinely fails, and in seven honest days one may, the test is not whether the app made you feel better. The test is whether, the next morning, the system let you resume without a hearing. That is the property — in the habit data, in the self-compassion data, and in the five appraisals themselves — that separates a tool for this fear from a decoration on top of it.
